en: As though an enemy had come to grapple with you.
From the wife you took under ancestral blessing,
You withheld your horse’s strength.
If you were ever a khan, it was in vain;
If you roar in anger,
You may cut off this poor head.
Among all your people filling Jeti-Özön,
Among the countless assembled throng,
My lord and hero, among your people
Was there no slave woman but me
For your mockery and amusement?
You hung that blood-spilling, keen-edged blade
From your wrist.
I see I was destined to suffer,
For rushing in heedlessly,
I see I was destined for disaster.
Cruel Aichürök, fair as the moon,
You are my treasure and my strength,
A bride lovely as the moon.
Delay brings grievous trouble—
I entrust Tootoru to you.
I gave you your choice from the herds;
Take my swift steed Tootoru.
I have been somewhat shamed, Aichürök;
Pour out my blood and take it in your leather flask!
Go to the herdsman and return;
Bring me quickly that poor fellow
Whom I found only when death was near.
Let my eyes behold him;
Bring him quickly back to me.”
Thus brave Kyyaz spoke,
Beginning a quarrel and hiding his intent,
Stirring up still greater trouble and strife:
“You were a lake, Chürök—overlook my fault!
Go safely and return unharmed;
Come back quickly and do not make me yearn.”
Thus he spoke to Chürök,
Striding away with wicked thoughts;
To the hapless woman fair as the moon
He entrusted the horse Tootoru.
Brave Kyyaz turned back,
Kyyaz the warrior with the fierce mustache;
When you looked at his mustache,
It resembled a sack from Bukhara.
Each of his shoulders was immense,
As though two men sat upon them;
When you looked at his two cheeks,
They were like two sated Dungans.
Such was his aspect when you saw him,
Like a bloodthirsty khan,
Like a mighty ruler of nations.
Kyyaz turned and remained behind,
Entrusting his bay horse:
If you will not ride him, here is the road;
If you would push him, here is the ravine;
If you would bind him, here are his legs.
Many are the cares within my heart;
God stands above your greatness.
Kyyaz, your anger has brought no good;
Time and again,
You have not curbed your violence.
Because my beast spoke,
You fly into a rage.
Let us pass before him,
Ask your beast to speak,
And, hero, though we are women,
Let us hear.”
She turned Tootoru’s mouth,
And before brave Kyyaz
Your dear sister-in-law Aichürök
Stood pulling the bay horse’s reins.
Wearing a robe patterned with blue flowers,
Brave Kyyaz, had you seen him,
Raged like a blue-maned lion;
He ran forward, heaving and panting,
His knees bending toward the ground,
His weapons set in order,
A naked sword strapped to him.
He pulled the reins
And turned the tireless steed Tootoru’s head.
Such was brave Kyyaz when you saw him;
As the bay horse swayed and plunged,
He stood stroking its forelock.
The great bay horse neighed,
But its forelock did not part,
And it showed no sign of speaking.
He turned it this way and stroked it,
But the great bay horse said nothing.
The bay horse had no words to speak,
And brave Kyyaz, enraged,
Was disgraced before Chürök,
The woman lovely as the moon.
“You said Tootoru had spoken—
I will smash you down upon the earth!
Across the rough and broken steppe,
Along ridges no horse can tread,
I will stretch my stride like an argali.
I will deliver punishment
To that deceitful, cunning woman!
If a ravine with cliff-bound hollows appears,
If a deadly mountain rises,
I will wheel and twist my neck.
That beautiful woman,
That cunning and clever infidel,
That woman with her tinkling laugh,
That infidel who thinks herself so bold—
If I do not veer and wrench my neck,
If I do not bring her crashing
Against the deep black earth below!
I will break her arms and leave them dangling;
That mincing wretch—
I will end her life in this fashion
And cast her sprawling on her back,
Unless I avenge the blow she struck me.
Though my flesh be torn apart like a sheep’s,
Though my path be straightened like a felt mat,
I will open my mouth like a cavern
And scatter blood-flecked white foam
Across my chest.
I will traverse the four corners
Of the whole round world forty times.
My back shall bend without arching,
My shriveled hooves
Shall spread as broad as a great cauldron.
I will stretch my mouth against the reins
Until I deliver your punishment;
I will bend my body from head to foot,
And make the woman who asked for the horse
Despair of her fly-sized life.
I will truly open your eyes,
Carry you off and subdue you,
And kill you.
I will run on and gouge you.”
Kyyaz returned to his throne.
At that moment Aichürök
Lashed the cloud-swift bay horse
Wildly from side to side,
Digging in her heels left and right,
And set out upon the road.
The ground crumbled beneath his tracks,
And he thundered faster as he went,
His soles pounding upon the earth,
The bit of black steel
Clanging in his throat.
Though only a beast, the great bay horse
Raced against the flying birds;
The pale reins, knotted at the grip,
Stretched taut between both hands
Of the terrified woman,
As she struggled with the bit
Of the plunging bay horse.
Wiser than a mere beast, Tootoru thought:
“If I do not twist my neck like a stag,
Suddenly bolt away
And dash her into a pit,
Until she is utterly smashed to pieces!
If I do not pour out your blood by the flaskful
And truly drain your strength,
You wicked daughter of Akun,
If I do not tear out your life!
If I do not cast you down and spill
Your black blood by the flaskful!
She wears a coat befitting a hero,
And mounts a mighty horse as though she were one.
The ravine is deep, the cliff sheer,
You accursed, blazing wretch,
You brazen woman,
Who deceived brave Kyyaz,
You surpassingly cunning infidel—
I shall wrench my neck like a stag.
If a cliff a spear’s height rises,
I shall leap without turning aside.
I shall dash her brains out on the stones,
He raced along the rugged slope.
The bay horse flew at a gallop,
And Aichürök upon his back
Despaired of her fragile life.
The white reins, knotted short,
Strained rigid in her hands when pulled.
The hostility of the masterless brute
Now plainly revealed itself.
He thundered onward like a flying cloud,
And wherever his hooves struck, the black earth
Burst apart on every side.
Truly, Chürök’s
Fragile soul cried out in terror.
He bolted wildly, snorting,
And raced headlong, bent on mischief;
That great bay horse, a veritable scourge,
Flew like a cloud.
“If I turn him aside, I am dead;
In this relentless place
I have seen what Tootoru can do,”
Thought Chürök, her soul nearly departing.
Tootoru bolted away,
Bringing cruel havoc;
He ran without swerving,
For Tootoru was a beast indeed,
While Aichürök upon his back
Despaired of her precious life.
Er Kyyaz’s bay horse Tootoru
Plainly showed his malice.
“If this bay horse has his way,
He will carry me into a fire-pit
That scorches the feet, and hurl me in;
He will carry me into a misery
No one can cross and escape;
He will carry me into a snare
From which no trapped soul can emerge;
He will carry me where the clear sky is veiled,
Into the enemy host, and cast me down.”
The noble but ill-fated woman
Thought long and hard:
“Those bulging eyes of yours—
I shall kill you myself!
If I cannot settle your account,
You accursed, demon-ridden beast,
If I cannot beat the frenzy out of you,
And dash your hide against the stones!
I shall subdue this woman,
Carry her off, and take her.
I shall bend the back and neck
Of this woman who thinks herself so strong;
I shall bring her untimely death,
And utterly thwart all her schemes;
I shall plunge her into chaos
And take my vengeance at last!”
So thinking, the charger
Lowered his head to the ground
And lengthened his stride beyond all measure.
His soles thundered upon the earth,
The bit of black steel
Clanged deep in his throat;
His mane and tail streamed wide,
His forelegs stabbed the ground,
His forelock parted across his brow,
And in the roaring brute
The marks of a true charger appeared.
His ribs drew taut,
His hooves bit into the ground,
His spine jutted out,
And his great bones bulged
As he raced onward thus.
He meant to twist his neck like a stag,
Swerve toward a pit as deep as a man is tall,
And cast himself into it,
To bring outright death
Upon moon-faced Chürök,
To find some means to destroy her
And wreak his fury at last.
Tootoru, wiser than a mere beast,
Struck all four hooves against the ground,
While his thick, armful of a tail
Became a horse lower than a swine.
She bound his forelegs and hindlegs fast,
And brought humiliation upon the bay horse.
